title: AI Is Hitting Paychecks Before Payrolls, New Labor Data Show
excerpt: Research from Apollo, Stanford and a 138-million-worker study finds pay growth running slower in AI-exposed occupations — with the lowest-paid workers taking the largest hit — even as employment holds steady.
body:
• Apollo Global Management's analysis of 321 occupations found wage growth in high-AI-exposure jobs ran 6.7 percentage points slower after 2023 — with no measurable decline in employment.
  • The lowest-paid workers absorb the largest hit: real wage growth trailed by 10.7% in the bottom earnings quartile, while top-quartile earners saw no significant effect.
  • Entry-level hiring is thinning fastest: among workers aged 22 to 25, employment in the most AI-exposed occupations runs 19% below less-exposed fields, driven entirely by fewer hires rather than layoffs.

The first place artificial intelligence is leaving its mark on the American workforce is not the unemployment rolls. It is in paychecks.

A wave of new labor-market research is shifting the AI-and-jobs debate away from mass layoffs and toward something quieter: wage compression. Employers are keeping headcounts largely intact while using AI-driven productivity gains to slow pay raises, hold down starting salaries and freeze hiring for the most exposed roles.

The evidence: slower pay growth, steady payrolls

The most direct evidence comes from Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok and researcher Sania Edlich, who matched 321 occupations against Bureau of Labor Statistics data from 2015 through 2025 using the Anthropic Economic Index, a measure of actual AI usage drawn from model interaction logs rather than theoretical exposure models. They found that wages in occupations highly exposed to AI grew 6.7% more slowly after 2023 than in low-exposure jobs, while employment levels showed no statistically significant change. In other words, the measurable effect so far is on wages, not jobs.

The burden is sharply uneven. Real wage growth in the bottom earnings quartile trailed low-exposure roles by 10.7%; the second and third quartiles trailed by 5.4% and 4.0%. Workers in the highest earnings quartile showed no statistically significant negative effect. An estimated 5.8 million U.S. workers — about 3.7% of the labor force — are already affected, representing roughly $28 billion in foregone annual labor income, according to the analysis.

New hires and young workers feel it first

Separate research points the same direction for people entering the workforce. A working paper by IESE researchers Mireia Gine and Jose Azar, with Javier Sanz-Espin of the Toulouse School of Management, tracked 138 million U.S. workers and found starting wages in AI-exposed companies fell 4.5% after the launch of ChatGPT, led by a 6.3% drop for junior positions. Starting salaries for mid-level roles declined 5.9%, while pay for senior-level hires held steady or rose.

Erik Brynjolfsson, director of the Stanford Digital Economy Lab, put the entry-level squeeze in plain terms at Stanford's recent Economic Summit: software developers aged 22 to 26 have seen roughly a 20% decline in entry-level hiring, and call centers about a 15% relative decline. "Mid-career people are doing okay. The more senior people are doing well," he said.

Stanford researchers using anonymized payroll data from ADP found employment among 22- to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations is now 19% lower than in less-exposed fields, up from a 13% gap a year earlier. The driver is not layoffs: existing employees are not being fired at higher rates. Employers have simply stopped hiring for those positions.

A Census Bureau analysis of the Quarterly Workforce Indicators tells a similar story at the firm level. In the most AI-exposed firms, early-career employment declined by 159,000 jobs, and the drop in hiring explains all of the loss. Separations actually declined, which cushioned the fall.

AI's impact so far has been more evident on employment, but "we're beginning to see a little bit of effect on wages, too." — Erik Brynjolfsson, Stanford Digital Economy Lab

Why wages, not jobs — yet

Economists caution that the data remain early and contested. A Bureau of Labor Statistics analysis of 18 AI-exposed occupations found only a 0.2% job decline as of May 2025, with overall payrolls still climbing. The Apollo researchers acknowledge their exposure measure rests on usage data from a single company and covers only a fraction of occupations. And a New York Fed analysis argues remote work, not AI, explains roughly two-thirds of the rise in unemployment among young college graduates since the pandemic.

What the studies agree on is the mechanism: generative AI automates the standardized cognitive tasks — drafting, summarizing, coding, basic analysis — that are concentrated in junior and mid-level roles. Companies capture the productivity gain by holding down pay and hiring rather than by cutting headcount, which keeps the headline unemployment rate low even as pay growth for exposed workers lags.

What to watch next

The next read comes from the wage data itself. Brynjolfsson said there is still insufficient data to fully measure AI's effect on pay, but that should change in coming months as labor-market trends emerge. Slok, for his part, argues the AI spending boom is simultaneously creating work: record business formation and rising demand for AI implementation talent, semiconductors and energy could offset losses through what economists call Jevons paradox — cheaper technology creating more demand for it.

For workers, the divide emerging in the data is not human versus machine. It is routine versus judgment. Roles built on negotiation, complex problem-solving and relationships sit on the safer side of the line; standardized tasks that AI can absorb sit on the other. Which side a job falls on increasingly determines what its paycheck does next.
